title: Tally Atoms in a Formula
statement:
You get a chemical-style formula as a string. It is built from these pieces:

  • An element: one uppercase letter followed by zero or more lowercase letters, like N, Fe or Uuo.
  • An optional count right after an element or a closing parenthesis: a number of 2 or more. No count means 1.
  • A group: a formula in parentheses, optionally followed by a count that multiplies everything inside. Groups can nest.

Return the total count of each element as one string: elements in sorted (alphabetical) order, each followed by its count, with the count left out when it is 1.

examples.why: The 3 after the group multiplies both S and O4, giving S3 and O12.
Counts multiply through every level: each C sits inside a 2 and a 3, so there are 6.
H and He are different elements. The two separate H's are added together.

constraints: formula is valid and uses only letters, digits, '(' and ')'
Every total count fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Ignore parentheses first. How do you read an element name and its count with one pointer?
A group's count applies to everything since its opening parenthesis. You need to set aside what was collected outside the group until the group closes.
Keep a stack of count maps. On ( push an empty map. On ), read the multiplier, pop the top map, multiply it, and add it into the map below. Elements always go into the top map.

explain.intuition:
Without parentheses this is just tokenizing: read an uppercase letter and the lowercase letters after it, read the digits after that, and add to a map. Parentheses change one thing: a count after ) applies to everything inside that group, and groups nest, so the most recently opened group is the first to close. That last-in, first-out shape is a stack.

Push a fresh map on (. Elements always go into the top map. On ), pop the group's map, multiply every count by the number that follows, and merge it into the map below. At the end one map is left with the totals. A recursive parser that returns a map per group is the same idea, with the call stack doing the work. It is the same shape as computing styles for nested DOM nodes, where an inner scope is merged into its parent when it closes.
steps: Start with a stack holding one empty map, and an index i = 0.
On (: push an empty map and move on.
On ): read the digits after it (1 if none), pop the top map, and add each count times the multiplier into the new top map.
Otherwise read an element name (uppercase, then lowercase letters) and its count (1 if none) and add it to the top map.
Sort the keys of the remaining map and join each name with its count, omitting counts of 1.
pitfalls: Reading only one letter per element. HHeH then looks like four elements H, H, e, H.
Reading only one digit. (N2)99 has a multiplier of 99, not 9.
Applying a group's multiplier to the whole formula so far, instead of only to the contents of that group.

complexity.time: O(n · d + k log k) for nesting depth d and k distinct elements

solutions.title: Recursive descent
solutions.idea: A function parses until ')' or the end and returns a map. On '(' it calls itself, then multiplies the returned map by the count after ')'.

solutions.title: Stack of count maps
solutions.idea: Push a map on '(', add elements to the top map, and on ')' pop, multiply and merge into the map below.

followups: Deep nesting makes every closing parenthesis re-multiply the whole inner map. How would parsing right to left with a running multiplier avoid that?
Report an error position for invalid input, like an unmatched parenthesis or a lowercase letter at the start.
